prompt.text: Which choice is an architecture decision rather than a coding detail?

options: Whether services share one database
How a button is named
Which loop style a function uses
The order of import statements

hints: Pick the choice that is hard to undo after launch.

teaching.text: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse later: boundaries, data ownership, communication and deployment. Naming and loop style are coding details because they are cheap to change.

prompt.text: An architecture is never finished; it keeps
as the system and its constraints change.

answer.text: An architecture is never finished; it keeps evolving as the system and its constraints change.

hints: Another word for changing over time.
cards.fullLine: An architecture is never finished; it keeps evolving as the system and its constraints change.

teaching.text: Architects do not produce a final diagram. They keep making and revising decisions as the product, the team and the load change.

cards.summary: A boundary is a clear interface

prompt.text: A boundary is useful when each side can change without breaking the other, so components should talk through a clear

answer.text: A boundary is useful when each side can change without breaking the other, so components should talk through a clear interface.

hints: The agreed contract between two parts.
cards.fullLine: A boundary is useful when each side can change without breaking the other, so components should talk through a clear interface.

teaching.text: A boundary hides an implementation behind a contract. The caller depends on the contract, not on the internals, so either side can be replaced.

teaching.alt: Two modules exchanging a message through a narrow interface while their insides change

cards.summary: A trade-off buys one quality with another

prompt.text: What does a design trade-off mean?

answer.text: Making one quality better by accepting less of another.

options: Making one quality better by accepting less of another
Finding a design with no downsides
Choosing the newest tool available
Adding every useful feature
correct: Making one quality better by accepting less of another

hints: Every real design gives something up.

teaching.text: Caching improves latency but adds staleness. Strong consistency improves correctness but costs availability during a partition. Naming the cost is part of the decision.

prompt.text: Two modules that must change together are tightly

answer.text: Two modules that must change together are tightly coupled.

cards.fullLine: Two modules that must change together are tightly coupled.

teaching.text: Coupling is not automatically bad. Some parts must coordinate. The problem is hidden coupling: a change in one place breaks a distant part with no clear contract.

cards.summary: Cohesion is one job done well

answer.text: One module does one related job well.

options: One module does one related job well
One module touches every part of the app
Two modules share one database
Every module uses the same framework
correct: One module does one related job well

hints: Cohesion is about what belongs together.

teaching.text: High cohesion keeps related rules in one place. Low cohesion scatters one job across many modules, so every change touches several files.

cards.summary: A stateless service keeps no session

prompt.text: A stateless service keeps no session
between requests, so any instance can serve the next one.

answer.text: A stateless service keeps no session state between requests, so any instance can serve the next one.

cards.fullLine: A stateless service keeps no session state between requests, so any instance can serve the next one.

teaching.text: Stateless services are easy to scale because the load balancer can send each request anywhere. Shared state moves to a database, cache or token.

prompt.text: Adding more machines to share the load is called scaling...

options: horizontally
vertically
diagonally
recursively

hints: Think of a row of servers side by side.

teaching.text: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger. Horizontal scaling adds more machines. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services and a way to balance traffic.

prompt.text: What one word describes a design that stays cheap to change over time?

hints: It starts with an e and rhymes with solvable.
cards.fullLine: A design that stays cheap to change over time is evolvable.

teaching.text: Evolvability is not about predicting the future. It is about keeping decisions reversible and boundaries clear enough that the next change stays small.

cards.summary: The same architecture can fit one team and fail another

prompt.text: Why can two teams copy the same architecture and get different results?

answer.text: Architecture must fit each team's constraints.

options: Architecture must fit each team's constraints
One team used the wrong editor
Architecture only works in the cloud
Results depend on the diagram tool
correct: Architecture must fit each team's constraints

hints: Team size, skills and budget matter as much as the pattern.

teaching.text: A pattern is advice, not a guarantee. The team's size, skills, budget and domain decide whether the same shape helps or hurts.
